label: thm:degreeone
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:degreeone}
For each coordinate curve class $e_i$ and all $n\geq4$,
\[
 N_{0,e_i}=(n-1)(n-2),\qquad N_{1,e_i}=-2(n-1)(n-2),\qquad
 N_{a,e_i}=0\quad(2\leq a\leq n-2).
\]
Therefore the coefficient of $Q$ in the diagonal descendant tuple is
\[
 n(n-1)(n-2)\,(1,-2,0,\ldots,0).
\]
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Fix $i$, put $Y_i=(\mathbb P^1)^{n-1}$, and let
$h=\sum_{j\ne i}p_j$. The equation of $F_n$ is
$x_0a_i+x_1b_i=0$ over $Y_i$. A coordinate fiber is contained in $F_n$
exactly on $S_i=\{a_i=b_i=0\}\subset Y_i$.
At a point of $S_i$, if $da_i,db_i$ were dependent, a nonzero combination
$x_0da_i+x_1db_i$ would vanish. At that point of $\mathbb P^1\times Y_i$ both
the fiber and base derivatives of the equation would vanish,
contradicting smoothness of $F_n$. Thus $S_i$ is a smooth regular
codimension-two locus of class $h^2$.

The ambient one-marked degree-one moduli is $\mathbb P^1\times Y_i$;
the hypersurface moduli is its zero locus $\mathbb P^1\times S_i$ for the induced section.
The degree-one nonconstant component maps isomorphically to its fiber.
A contracted tree attached to it cannot be stable with only one marking:
for a nonempty subtree with $v\geq1$ vertices and at most one marking, the total
number of special points is at most $2(v-1)+1+1=2v<3v$.
There are consequently no such boundary trees and no residual
map automorphisms. This description also holds for families, since
a fiberwise degree-one map to $\mathbb P^1$ identifies the universal domain
with the trivial $\mathbb P^1$-bundle, with its marking specifying a point.

The induced rank-two positive-bundle section on the smooth ambient
moduli has regular zero locus $\mathbb P^1\times S_i$; its virtual class
is therefore fundamental. The local obstruction bundle has rank
$m-1=0$, so the local virtual class is fundamental as well.
On this moduli space let $p$ be the class of the marked point in the
fiber. The universal cotangent line has $\psi=-2p$, and
$\operatorname{ev}_{F_n}^*H=p+h$, with $p^2=0$.
Since $\int_{S_i}h^{n-3}=\int_{Y_i}h^{n-1}=(n-1)!$, the primary invariant is
$(n-1)!/(n-3)!=(n-1)(n-2)$, the first descendant is
$-2(n-1)!/(n-3)!$, and the remaining ones vanish by $p^2=0$.
There are $n$ coordinate classes, giving the final assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:degreetwo
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:degreetwo}
For all $n\geq4$ and distinct $i,j$,
\[
 N_{0,2e_i}=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}4,\qquad
 N_{0,e_i+e_j}=-2(n-1)(n-2).
\]
Consequently, writing $N_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}N_{0,\beta}$,
\[
 N_2=-\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(4n-5)}4.
\]
The multiple-cover transform defined by
$N_{0,\beta}=\sum_{k\alpha=\beta}b_\alpha/k^2$ gives
\[
 b_{2e_i}=0,\qquad b_{e_i+e_j}=-2(n-1)(n-2),\qquad
 n_2:=\sum_{|\beta|=2}b_\beta=-n(n-2)(n-1)^2.
\]
These explicit integrality statements require no general integrality theorem.
head: environment
name: Degree-two primaries

title: Démonstration
body_md:
On the ambient moduli use the bundles $E_+=\pi_*f^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)$ and
$E_-=R^1\pi_*f^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(-H)$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:basechange}.
The virtual comparison computes the invariant by integrating
$e(E_+)e(E_-)\operatorname{ev}^*\delta_0$. We compute the two possible degree types.

For $2e_i$, separate the passive factor $(\mathbb P^1)^{n-1}$ and write
$\bar p=\sum_{j\ne i}p_j$. On the active unmarked moduli
$M=\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(\mathbb P^1,2)$ put
\[
 E^{\rm act}_+=\pi_*f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1),\qquad
 E^{\rm act}_-=R^1\pi_*f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1),\qquad c=c_1(E^{\rm act}_-).
\]
These have ranks three and one. The line bundles on the target are
$\mathcal O(1)$ and $\mathcal O(-1)$, whose pullbacks have degrees
$2$ and $-2$. Let $B$ be the trace-free line of the double cover
recalled below (unrelated to the bundles $\mathcal B_\pm$ on $Y_n$), so that $f_*\mathcal O_C=\mathcal O\oplus
(\mathcal O(-1)\otimes B)$. The projection formula gives
\[
 E^{\rm act}_+=H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(1))\otimes\mathcal O\oplus B,
 \qquad
 E^{\rm act}_-=H^1(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-2))\otimes B\cong B,
\]
so $E^{\rm act}_+\cong\mathcal O^2\oplus E^{\rm act}_-$ and
$c_1(E^{\rm act}_+)=c$.
After passive twisting,
\[
 e(E_+)e(E_-)=\bar p^2(\bar p+c)(c-\bar p)=c^2\bar p^2-\bar p^4.
\]
Here and below these bundles pull back under forgetting the marking;
contraction of an unstable degree-zero component preserves their cohomology.

We give the stack integral used in this computation. An unmarked degree-two
map to $\mathbb P^1$ has no contracted components, since a contracted subtree
attached to the at most two positive components cannot have three special
points per vertex.
It is a finite flat double cover, including the reducible
boundary consisting of two degree-one components. Conversely every
nonzero binary quadratic defines such a cover; a double root gives the
nodal reducible cover. Trace splitting of the rank-two algebra gives
$\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1)\otimes B$ over a base, with multiplication
specified by a section of $\mathcal O(2)\otimes B^{-2}$.
This description is compatible with base change (the finite morphism is
flat of degree two, and the trace-free line has relative degree $-1$).
It identifies
\[
 M\cong[(H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(2))\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb G_m]
       =\mathbb P(2,2,2).
\]
The branch map to $\mathbb P^2$ has generic stabilizer $\mu_2$.
If $h$ is the pullback of its hyperplane class, the character line
$E^{\rm act}_-$ has $c=\pm h/2$, as also follows by tensoring the trace splitting
with $\mathcal O(-1)$ and taking $H^1$.
Thus
$\int_M c^2=\frac12\frac14=\frac18$.
The divisor equation (Appendix~\ref{app:forget}) for the marking gives
$\int_{\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,1}(\mathbb P^1,2)}\operatorname{ev}^*p_i\,c^2=2/8$.
Only the term $p_i\bar p^{\,n-3}/(n-3)!$ of $\delta_0$ contributes,
since the other terms have excessive passive degree.
Because $\int_{(\mathbb P^1)^{n-1}}\bar p^{\,n-1}=(n-1)!$,
the answer is $(n-1)(n-2)/4$.

For $e_i+e_j$, the active unmarked moduli is $\mathbb P^3$, the complete
linear system of $(1,1)$ divisors in $Y_A=\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$.
Every geometric map has at most two positive components. A contracted
unmarked subtree would need at least three external attachments by
stability, so none occurs. The map is the inclusion of a smooth graph
or the transverse nodal union of one fiber of each ruling.
Every automorphism of such an inclusion is the identity.

For a family over $S$, the map $C\to Y_A\times S$ is proper and
fiberwise quasi-finite, hence finite. The cokernel of
$\mathcal O_{Y_A\times S}\to f_*\mathcal O_C$ vanishes on fibers;
Nakayama, applied to this finite module locally, makes it zero.
The map is therefore a closed immersion. Its flat finitely presented
image is fiberwise an effective Cartier divisor, and the fiberwise
Cartier criterion makes it a relative effective Cartier divisor.
Its equation determines a line in the fixed four-dimensional space
$H^0(Y_A,\mathcal O(1,1))$, giving the projective-space functor.
These constructions commute with base change; the finite-presentation
data can first be descended to a Noetherian base if required.
This proves the stack isomorphism, including all finite stabilizers,
which here are trivial.

The one-marked moduli is the universal divisor
$U\subset\mathbb P^3\times Y_A$ by the stable-map universal-curve theorem
\cite[Proposition 4.5 and Corollary 4.6]{BM}.
A point at the node represents the map obtained by inserting a contracted
$\mathbb P^1$ between the two branches and placing the marking on it.
The two nodes and the marking make that component stable. Forgetting
the marking contracts it. A section through a node before this insertion
is not an admissible marked prestable curve. Pullback target bundles
retain their cohomology under the contraction, because the contracted
component has $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^1(\mathcal O)=0$ and values
match at its two nodes.
Let $h=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1))$ and
$\bar p=\sum_{k\ne i,j}p_k$, a sum of $n-2$ passive classes.
The universal divisor sequences give
\[
 c(E^{\rm act}_+)=(1-h)^{-1},\qquad E^{\rm act}_-=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(-1).
\]
Indeed, for the positive bundle the sequence has first term
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(-1)\boxtimes\mathcal O$ and middle term
$\mathcal O\boxtimes\mathcal O(1,1)$; for the negative bundle the first
term is $\mathcal O(-h)\boxtimes\mathcal O(-2,-2)$ and the middle term
is $\mathcal O\boxtimes\mathcal O(-1,-1)$.
Their direct images give precisely the two assertions. Hence
\[
 e(E_+)e(E_-)=-(\bar p^4+2h\bar p^3+2h^2\bar p^2+2h^3\bar p),\qquad h^4=0.
\]
Integrate this against $(\bar p+p_i+p_j)^{n-2}/(n-2)!$ on $U$ times
the passive factors, using $[U]=h+p_i+p_j$.
Only two terms survive. The term $-2h^3\bar p$ combines with
$p_i+p_j$ from $[U]$ and the linear active term of the insertion,
giving $-4(n-2)$. The term $-2h^2\bar p^2$ combines with $h$ from $[U]$
and the quadratic active term, giving $-2(n-2)(n-3)$.
Their sum is $-2(n-1)(n-2)$, as asserted.
There are $n$ classes of the first type and $\binom{n}{2}$ of the
second. Sum them, and subtract $N_{0,e_i}/4$ in class $2e_i$ to obtain
the multiple-cover claims.
head: environment

label: thm:supportbound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:supportbound}
Let $\beta=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ have total degree $m>0$ and let
$k=\#\{i:d_i>0\}$. For the insertions defined here,
\[
 N_{a,\beta}=0\quad\hbox{if }a>2m+k-2.
\]
In particular $N_{a,\beta}=0$ if $a>3m-2$. At degree two this gives
$N_{a,\beta}=0$ for $a\geq5$; these assertions are understood within
$0\leq a\leq n-2$.
head: environment
name: Support bound for descendants

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Every passive coordinate is constant on the connected genus-zero domain. This is
functorial over arbitrary bases since $\pi_*\mathcal O_C= \mathcal O_B$. At any
geometric base point, choose an affine chart containing the constant fiber
image. Properness of the universal curve makes the image of the complement
closed in the base. Removing it puts the whole family over that neighborhood in
the chart, where $\pi_*\mathcal O_C=\mathcal O_B$ gives the factorization. The
local factorizations glue uniquely. Here $R^1\pi_*\mathcal O_C=0$ and the
isomorphism $\mathcal O_B\to\pi_*\mathcal O_C$ follow by the same split-complex
argument as Lemma~\ref{lem:basechange}, since each connected genus-zero fiber
has $h^0=1$, $h^1=0$, and the constant section generates $H^0$. Thus the ambient
one-marked moduli is
\[
 \overline{\mathcal M}_{0,1}((\mathbb P^1)^k,\beta_{\rm act})
             \times(\mathbb P^1)^{n-k}.
\]
Stability and the cotangent line depend only on the active map.
The active moduli is a smooth proper Deligne--Mumford stack of dimension
$k-3+2m+1=2m+k-2$, since the target is convex and the genus-zero obstruction
$H^1(C,f^*T)$ vanishes. 
Its rational Chow groups vanish above this
dimension, so $\psi^a=0$ there for the stated range. Pull back and use
the ambient virtual comparison; multiplying by its Euler classes and
the insertion cannot change this zero. Finally $k\leq m$.
head: environment

label: prop:sharpbound
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sharpbound}
For $m\geq1$ and $n\geq3m$,
\[
 [Q^m]\mathcal D_{3m-2}^\Delta(Q)
 =-\frac{2^mn!}{m!\,(n-3m)!}\ne0.
\]
Thus $3m-2$ cannot be replaced by $2m$ as a uniform descendant cutoff.
For example, $n=9$, $m=3$ gives
$[Q^3]\mathcal D_7^\Delta=-483840$, although $7>2m$.
head: environment
name: Sharp diagonal bound

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Work with the local ambient $I$-series at $z=1$ and remove its bare
exponential $e^{H\log y}$. For a degree tuple of total degree $m$
and support $k$, the local numerator has degree at most $2m$ in $H$.
Because $p_i^2=0$, expanding each active denominator contributes at most
one power of $p_i$, hence at most $k$ additional cohomological powers.
The total degree is at most $2m+k\leq3m$.
A coefficient of $y^r$ in $e^{-Hg(y)}$ has degree at most $r$ in $H$.
For $r>0$, its product with a term of degree $m-r$ has degree at most
$3(m-r)+r<3m$. Thus normalization cannot change the top coefficient.
Neither can substituting $y(Q)=Q+O(Q^2)$, since lower degrees have
cohomological degree strictly less than $3m$.

The top degree is possible only for tuples with $m$ distinct entries
one. For each such tuple the leading numerator is $(-1)^mH^{2m}$,
and the top denominator term is $(-2)^m\prod_{i:d_i=1}p_i$.
Summing over these subsets gives
$2^mH^{2m}e_m(p)=2^mH^{3m}/m!$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:extraction} with $a=3m-2$.
head: environment

label: thm:compact
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:compact}
One has
\[
 Z\setminus D_\infty=X_n,\quad [D_\infty]=\xi,\quad i_0^*\xi=0,\quad
 \mathcal O_Z(D_\infty)|_{D_\infty}=K_{F_n}^{-1},\quad c_1(TZ)=2\xi.
\]
The class $\xi$ is nef. For every positive $\beta$ and every $\ell\geq0$,
\[
 \overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(X_n,\beta)
 \cong\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(Z,i_{0*}\beta)
\]
with their standard obstruction theories, virtual classes, and virtual
structure sheaves. Moreover
\[
 H_2(Z,\mathbb Z)=i_{0*}H_2(F_n,\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\ell_f,\qquad\xi\cdot\ell_f=1,
\]
and $k\mathfrak b=i_{0*}\beta$ if and only if $\mathfrak b=i_{0*}\alpha$ and
$k\alpha=\beta$. For such classes, $\mathfrak b$ is effective if and only if
$\alpha$ is effective.
head: environment
name: Compactification and class comparison

title: Démonstration
body_md:
A line with nonzero first coordinate has a unique representative
$(1,v)$, identifying the open complement with $K_{F_n}$.
Projection of the tautological subline to $\mathcal O_{F_n}$ cuts out
$D_\infty$, proving its divisor class and its restriction to the
zero section. On the infinity section the tautological subline is
$K_{F_n}$, giving the displayed positive normal bundle.
The relative Euler sequence gives
$c_1(T_{Z/F_n})=2\xi+p^*c_1(K_{F_n})$; adding $p^*c_1(T_{F_n})$ leaves $2\xi$.
The dual bundle $\mathcal O_{F_n}\oplus K_{F_n}^{-1}$ is globally generated,
and surjects onto $\mathcal O_Z(1)$, so $\xi$ is nef.

A curve not contained in $D_\infty$ has nonnegative intersection with
that effective divisor, and a nonconstant curve contained in it has
strictly positive intersection because $K_{F_n}^{-1}$ is ample.
In a stable map of class $i_{0*}\beta$ the total $\xi$-degree is zero.
Every nonconstant component must therefore avoid $D_\infty$.
A contracted component in $D_\infty$ would connect, through contracted
components, to a nonconstant component meeting it, which is impossible.
Thus every geometric map lands in $X_n$.
For families, maps with image in an open target form an open substack:
the bad locus is the proper image from the universal curve of the
inverse image of $D_\infty$. It has no geometric points by the preceding
argument and hence is empty, over arbitrary bases. The open immersion
of moduli stacks is therefore an isomorphism including nilpotents.
Since $T_Z|_{X_n}=T_{X_n}$, the actual obstruction complexes and their maps
agree; the virtual classes and the virtual structure sheaves agree too.

The projective-bundle formula and the section give the direct-sum
lattice decomposition. Intersecting $k\mathfrak b=i_{0*}\beta$ with $\xi$
annihilates the fiber coefficient, and projection to $F_n$ gives
$k\alpha=\beta$. For effectivity, one implication uses the zero
section. Conversely push an effective cycle of class $i_{0*}\alpha$
to $F_n$; its pushforward is an effective cycle of class $\alpha$.
This is a statement about effective cycles, not an assertion that
all such classes have nonempty genus-zero stable-map moduli.
head: environment

label: rem:semipositive
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:semipositive}
Algebraically, $c_1(TZ)=2\xi$ is nef. The symplectic hypothesis in
Theorem~\ref{thm:IP} below is different, because in complex
dimension $n$ there must be no spherical class $\mathfrak a$ with positive
symplectic area and $3-n\leq c_1(\mathfrak a)<0$.
For $n=4$ the only forbidden value is $-1$, impossible since $c_1(TZ)$
is even. For $n\geq5$, the classes
\[
 \mathfrak a_k=i_{0*}(k e_i)-\ell_f
\]
have $c_1(\mathfrak a_k)=-2$ and positive area for all sufficiently large $k$,
for every fixed Kähler form on $Z$. 
They are spherical, since coordinate curves in $F_n$ exist by Theorem~\ref{thm:degreeone}, as their parameter scheme has nonzero class $h^2$, and the fiber is a sphere.
The image of $\pi_2(Z)\to H_2(Z,\mathbb Z)$ is a subgroup, so their indicated difference
is spherical. Thus $Z$ fails this symplectic condition for $n\geq5$.
The existence of these topological classes does not say that they are
represented by holomorphic curves for the algebraic complex structure.
head: environment
name: Positivity and the scope of the arithmetic theorems

label: thm:CYcover
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:CYcover}
There is a smooth connected projective $n$-fold $\widetilde Z$,
a finite flat double cover $r:\widetilde Z\to Z$, and disjoint
divisors $F_{n,+},F_{n,-}\cong F_n$ over $D_0$, such that
\[
 K_{\widetilde Z}\cong\mathcal O_{\widetilde Z},\qquad
 N_{F_{n,\pm}/\widetilde Z}\cong K_{F_n} .
\]
Write $q=p\circ r$ and $j_\pm:F_n\hookrightarrow\widetilde Z$.
For every $\beta>0$ and $\ell\geq0$,
\[
 \overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(\widetilde Z,j_{+*}\beta)
 \cong\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(F_n,\beta)
 \cong\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(X_n,\beta),
\]
with the standard obstruction theories on the first and last stacks
identified. The virtual classes and virtual structure sheaves agree.
Every effective integral covering root of $j_{+*}\beta$ is
$j_{+*}\alpha$ with $k\alpha=\beta$; conversely each effective such
$\alpha$ gives a covering root. The same assertion holds modulo torsion.
head: environment
name: Calabi--Yau double cover and isolation of the local sector

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Write $\mathcal O_{F_n}(H)=K_{F_n}^{-1}$, which is very ample, and put
$M=\mathcal O_Z(2\xi)=-K_Z$.
Indeed the relative tangent determinant is
$\det T_{Z/F_n}=\mathcal O_Z(2\xi)\otimes p^*K_{F_n}$;
multiplication by $p^*\det T_{F_n}$ cancels the $K_{F_n}$ factor.
Thus, the canonical bundle $K_Z$ is isomorphic to the line bundle $\mathcal{O}_Z(-2\xi)$.
In the lines convention, the two tautological projections give sections
\[
 u\in H^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z(\xi)),\qquad
 v\in H^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z(\xi)\otimes p^*K_{F_n}).
\]
They never vanish simultaneously; $D_\infty=(u=0)$ and $D_0=(v=0)$.

Choose $a\in H^0(F_n,\mathcal O_{F_n}(4H))$ with smooth zero divisor.
Existence can be seen directly, without invoking a smoothness assertion
for an arbitrary semiample system. Embed $F_n$ by the very ample
$\mathcal O_{F_n}(4H)$ in $\mathbb P^N$. If the hyperplane corresponding to a
section is singular at a point $x$, it contains the projective tangent
$(n-1)$-plane $T_xF$. The incidence variety of such pairs has dimension
$n-1+(N-n)=N-1$ and is projective over the dual $\mathbb P^N$. Its image is
therefore a proper closed subset. Hence a hyperplane outside this image
has smooth section. The section is nonempty since an ample divisor on the
positive-dimensional projective variety $F_n$ has positive intersection
with $H^{n-2}$.

The section
\[
 b=u^4+p^*a\,v^4\in H^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z(4\xi))=H^0(Z,M^2)
\]
has smooth nonempty zero divisor $B$ disjoint from $D_0$.
Indeed, on $u\ne0$ its equation is $1+a w^4=0$, where $w=v/u$
is the fiber coordinate of $K_{F_n}$. On its zero set $aw\ne0$,
so the fiber derivative $4aw^3$ does not vanish.
On $v\ne0$ the equation in a local trivialization is $t^4+a=0$.
If $t\ne0$ its fiber derivative is nonzero; if $t=0$, smoothness
of $(a=0)$ gives a nonzero base derivative.
This proves smoothness everywhere, including along infinity.

Define
\[
 \widetilde Z=\operatorname{Spec}_Z(\mathcal O_Z\oplus M^{-1}),
 \qquad M^{-1}\otimes M^{-1}\xrightarrow{\,b\,}\mathcal O_Z.
\]
Locally the equation is $\tau^2=b$; hence the morphism is finite flat
of degree two and the total space is projective.
Away from $B$ it is étale. On $B$, its equation has nonzero base
differential $db$, so $\widetilde Z$ is smooth.
The section $b$ has a zero of order one along a branch component,
so it cannot be a square in the function field after a rational
trivialization of $M$. The generic cover is a field extension.
The algebra is locally free over the integral $Z$, and embeds in that
field, proving that $\widetilde Z$ is integral and thus connected.

Viewed as the hypersurface $\tau^2-b=0$ in $\operatorname{Tot}(M)$,
its canonical bundle is
\[
 K_{\widetilde Z}
  =r^*(K_Z\otimes M^{-1}\otimes M^2)
  =r^*(K_Z\otimes M)=\mathcal O_{\widetilde Z}.
\]
This follows from the tangent determinant sequence for the smooth hypersurface,
just as in Proposition~\ref{prop:geometry}. Equivalently, if $R_b=(\tau=0)$ is
the ramification divisor, the local equation $b=\tau^2$ gives $db=2\tau\,d\tau$
and hence $K_{\widetilde Z}=r^*K_Z\otimes\mathcal O(R_b)$. The tautological
section $\tau$ of $r^*M$ has divisor $R_b$, so this again gives the trivial
canonical line bundle. This computation proves an isomorphism of line bundles,
establishing more than the vanishing of a rational Chern class. Along $D_0$, $u$
trivializes $\mathcal O_Z(\xi)$ and $b=u^4$. Consequently $r^{-1}(D_0)$ is the
disjoint union $\tau=+u^2$ and $\tau=-u^2$, each isomorphic to $F_n$.
\'Etaleness along both components identifies their normal bundles with
$N_{D_0/Z}=K_{F_n}$. In particular
\begin{equation}\label{e:intersection_numbers}
 F_{n,+}\cdot j_{+*}\alpha=-H\cdot\alpha,\qquad
 F_{n,+}\cdot j_{-*}\alpha=0,\qquad q_*j_{\pm*}=\operatorname{id}.
\end{equation}

Now let a family of stable maps have class $j_{+*}\beta$.
Composition with the finite morphism $r$ preserves stability:
exactly the same components are contracted, and a nonconstant map
still has finite automorphism group.
Its class on $Z$ is $i_{0*}\beta$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:compact}, followed by zero-section factorization,
shows that this composed map factors scheme-theoretically through $D_0$.
The original map therefore factors through
$r^{-1}(D_0)=F_{n,+}\amalg F_{n,-}$ over the entire base.
For a geometric fiber the connected domain lies in one component.
The intersection numbers in eq.~\eqref{e:intersection_numbers} and $H\cdot\beta>0$ exclude $F_{n,-}$.
For a family, the two alternatives define open-and-closed subsets of the
base. Equivalently, the two idempotents pull back through
$\pi_*\mathcal O_C=\mathcal O_S$.
Since no geometric fiber lies in $F_{n,-}$, the entire family lies in $F_{n,+}$.
This proves the asserted stack isomorphism over arbitrary bases.

Along $F_{n,+}$ the differential $dr$ is an isomorphism
$j_+^*T_{\widetilde Z}\cong i_0^*T_Z=T_{F_n}\oplus K_{F_n}$.
It identifies the universal stable-map obstruction morphisms,
because they are induced by the same composed universal differential.
For an explicit comparison, let $\mathfrak M$ be the common stable-map
stack, let $\mathfrak B$ be the same smooth prestable-curve stack used
above, and let $\pi:\mathcal C\to\mathfrak M$ be the universal curve.
Composition with $r$ does not stabilize or alter this curve. The
obstruction morphisms fit into the commuting diagram
\begin{equation}\label{eq:CYcoverPOT}
\begin{array}{ccc}
 (R\pi_*f_Z^*T_Z)^\vee&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }&
 (R\pi_*f_{\widetilde Z}^*T_{\widetilde Z})^\vee\\[2mm]
 \phi_Z\downarrow&&\downarrow\phi_{\widetilde Z}\\[1mm]
 \mathbb L_{\mathfrak M/\mathfrak B}&\xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{id}\ }&
 \mathbb L_{\mathfrak M/\mathfrak B}.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
The chain rule for the universal differential, followed by the same
relative-duality and trace construction on $\mathcal C$, proves commutativity.
Global resolutions are supplied by \cite[Proposition 5]{BehrendGW}. Restriction
through the open immersion $X_n\subset Z$ makes the same comparison with the
theory of $X_n$. Thus the theories agree with those of \(X_n\), including their
maps to the cotangent complex.
Consequently, the induced isomorphism of stable-map stacks identifies the
perfect obstruction theories and hence the associated virtual classes and
virtual structure sheaves. The standard theory of \(F_n\), by contrast, has the
excess factor described in Theorem~\ref{thm:virtual} and
Remark~\ref{rem:localKexcess}.

Finally suppose $k\gamma=j_{+*}\beta$ and $\gamma$ is effective.
Set $\alpha=q_*\gamma$; then $k\alpha=\beta$.
The torsion-free splitting of $H_2(Z)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:compact}
gives $r_*\gamma=i_{0*}\alpha$.
Represent $\gamma$ by an effective cycle. Nefness of $r^*\xi$
and zero total degree force every component downstairs into $D_0$,
by the curve argument in that theorem. More explicitly, a complete
irreducible curve of zero $\xi$-degree avoids $D_\infty$ and hence
lies in $X_n$. On its normalization, a nonconstant projection to $F_n$
pulls $K_{F_n}$ back to a negative-degree line bundle, whose section is
zero. A curve projecting to a point cannot be complete and nonconstant
inside an affine-line fiber. Thus every such curve lies in $D_0$;
this argument applies to effective cycles of any geometric genus.
Thus the cycle splits between $F_{n,+}$ and $F_{n,-}$; write its projected
effective classes as $\alpha_+$ and $\alpha_-$.
Equation~\eqref{e:intersection_numbers} gives
$H\cdot\alpha_+=H\cdot\beta/k=H\cdot\alpha$.
Since $\alpha=\alpha_++\alpha_-$, ampleness forces $\alpha_-=0$.
The cycle lies in $F_{n,+}$, so $\gamma=j_{+*}\alpha$.
Conversely the inclusion preserves effectivity.
The proof still works if the initial equality is modulo torsion:
intersection numbers kill torsion, $H_2(Z)$ is free, and
$q_*j_{+*}=\operatorname{id}$ with free $H_2(F_n)$ gives the same
conclusion. In particular there are no additional effective torsion
lifts contributing to the invariants in this sector.

label: lem:formalCYsector
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Formal realization of the local neighborhood

title: Démonstration
body_md:
On $u\ne0$ write $w=v/u$ and $\eta=\tau/u^2$. The product $a w^4$
is a global regular function, although $w$ is locally the coordinate of
$K_{F_n}$. The equation of the cover is $\eta^2=1+a w^4$. In the completion
along the zero section the unique root with constant term $+1$ is
\[
 \eta=(1+a w^4)^{1/2}
      =\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{1/2}{j}(a w^4)^j.
\]
This converges in the ideal-adic topology and is compatible on every
infinitesimal neighborhood. Uniqueness also follows because the sum of
two roots with constant term $1$ is a unit. Since $a w^4$ is global,
the expressions glue and supply the inverse to the completed morphism $r$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The scheme $Z$ is an open-embedding compactification of $X_n$.
The variety $\widetilde Z$ is a compact target realizing the local
stable-map sector, with the formal-neighborhood identification just
proved. No isomorphism of an entire Zariski-open neighborhood of $F_{n,+}$
with all of $X_n$ is needed or asserted. The direct family argument in
Theorem~\ref{thm:CYcover} already establishes the sector over arbitrary
bases; the formal calculation is an additional description.
head: environment
name: A compact sector, not an asserted global open embedding

label: thm:integrality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:integrality}
There are unique rational numbers $b_\beta$, with the zero convention
for noneffective classes, such that
\[
 N_{0,\beta}=\sum_{k\alpha=\beta}\frac{b_\alpha}{k^2},\qquad
 b_\beta=\sum_{k\alpha=\beta}\frac{\mu(k)}{k^2}N_{0,\alpha}.
\]
Here $k$ is a positive integer, $\alpha$ is an integral curve class,
and $\mu$ is the arithmetic Mobius function. With
$N_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}N_{0,\beta}$ and
$n_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}b_\beta$, one has the formal identities
\begin{align}
 \mathcal D_0^\Delta(Q)&=\sum_{m\geq1}n_m\operatorname{Li}_2(Q^m),\label{eq:Li2}\\
 N_m&=\sum_{k\mid m}\frac{n_{m/k}}{k^2},\qquad
 n_m=\sum_{k\mid m}\frac{\mu(k)}{k^2}N_{m/k}\in\mathbb Q.\label{eq:mobius}
\end{align}
These statements alone make no integrality or enumerative assertion.
head: environment
name: Primary transform

title: Démonstration
body_md:
In a nonzero nonnegative degree tuple, any integral root has order
dividing its total degree. There are therefore finitely many roots.
The term $k=1$ defines $b_\beta$ inductively. Substitution of the proposed
inverse gives the coefficient
$r^{-2}\sum_{k\mid r}\mu(k)$ in front of $N_{0,\beta/r}$.
It is one for $r=1$ and zero otherwise. If $r>1$, expanding
$\prod_{p\mid r}(1-1)$ proves the last assertion. This proves the
inverse without an external inversion theorem. A multiple of an
effective class is effective, so the zero convention is consistent.
The number of tuples at a fixed total degree is finite. Summation over
them and the defining series $\operatorname{Li}_2(q)=\sum_{k\geq1}q^k/k^2$ give~\eqref{eq:Li2}--\eqref{eq:mobius}.

title: Démonstration

$\operatorname{ch}(1-[\mathcal P_i^{-1}])=1-e^{-p^*p_i}=p^*p_i$ exactly.

label: thm:chou
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:chou}
In that setting let $\beta\ne0$ be a positive integral curve class,
$\gamma\in H^{2(d-K_M\cdot\beta-2)}(M)$ homogeneous, and
$\Gamma=\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(\gamma)\in K^0(M)_\mathbb Q$. Then
\[
 \mathrm{GV}_\beta(\gamma)=\mathrm{QK}_\beta(\Gamma)
 +\delta_{K_M\cdot\beta,0}
  \sum_{\substack{r\mid\operatorname{ind}(\beta)\\r>1}}
                          \mu(r)r\,\mathrm{QK}_{\beta/r}(\Gamma),
\]
where $\operatorname{ind}(\beta)=\max\{r\geq1:\beta/r\in H_2(M,\mathbb Z)\}$,
$\mathrm{QK}$ is the true one-point genus-zero quantum-$K$ invariant, and
$\mathrm{GV}$ uses primary weight $r^{-2}$ in the zero-Chern sector and
equals $\mathrm{GW}$ in the positive-Chern sector.
head: environment

label: thm:QK
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Quantum-$K$ expression

title: Démonstration
body_md:
On $\widetilde Z$ use the integral algebraic class $r^*E_\delta$.
Its full character is $q^*\delta_0$, with complex degree $n-2$.
Since $\widetilde Z$ is a smooth projective variety, its underlying space
has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, and the Chern character
$\operatorname{ch}:K^0_{\mathrm{top}}(\widetilde Z)\otimes\mathbb Q\to H^{\mathrm{even}}(\widetilde Z,\mathbb Q)$
is an isomorphism. Thus the equality of characters identifies the image of
$r^*E_\delta$ with the rational topological class
$\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(q^*\delta_0)$ required by Chou's Proposition~3.4.
The target is smooth projective, dimension $n\geq4$, and $c_1=0$;
both symplectic and algebraic positivity conditions hold automatically.
Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:chou} applies without a nef-scope extension. Theorem~\ref{thm:CYcover} identifies the
moduli and actual obstruction theories for all effective roots with
those on $Z$ and $X_n$. Consequently their virtual structure sheaves
and the insertions agree, so their true quantum-$K$ invariants are
precisely the $\kappa_\alpha$ defined above.

                                                                   
                                          
The retraction $q_*$ to
$H_2(F_n,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^n$ shows that the divisibility index of $j_{+*}\beta$
is exactly that of $\beta$. The effective-root proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:CYcover} shows that passing to this quotient introduces
no extra effective class or stable-map component in the sector at hand.
Thus every root in the source formula is exactly accounted for.
The GV coefficients in the cited proposition are defined by the same
one-primary $k^{-2}$ transform as Theorem~\ref{thm:integrality}.
Uniqueness of that rational transform identifies them with $b_\beta$.
The first equality in~\eqref{eq:QKformula} is therefore the cited proposition.
The convolution of $k\mapsto k$ and $k\mapsto\mu(k)k$ at $r$ is
$r\sum_{k\mid r}\mu(k)$, which gives the inverse equality.
This also proves integrality directly from true $K$-theoretic Euler
characteristics, independently of the symplectic integrality route.

label: cor:primaryintegral
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:primaryintegral}
For every $n\geq4$, $b_\beta\in\mathbb Z$ and $n_m\in\mathbb Z$.
head: environment
name: Primary integrality in every loop order

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:QK} writes $b_\beta$ as the finite sum
$\sum_{k\alpha=\beta}\mu(k)k\,\kappa_\alpha$ of integers, because the
$\kappa_\alpha$ are true coherent Euler characteristics on proper
Deligne--Mumford stacks. Finite summation at fixed $H$-degree gives
$n_m\in\mathbb Z$. This proof uses the compact sector, the exact integral
$K$-lift, and Chou's one-primary identity, but neither a mirror theorem
nor an algebraic--symplectic comparison.
head: environment
name: Algebraic proof

label: thm:IP
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:IP}
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed semipositive symplectic manifold of real
dimension $2d\geq6$ and let
$\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k\in H^{\mathrm{even}}(M,\mathbb Z)$ be integral
primary insertions of even degree. Define $n_{\mathfrak a,0}$ in the zero-Chern
sector by
\[
 \sum_{\mathfrak a\ne0,\ c_1(\mathfrak a)=0}
   \mathrm{GW}_{\mathfrak a,0}(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k)q^{\mathfrak a}
 =\sum_{\mathfrak a\ne0,\ c_1(\mathfrak a)=0}
   n_{\mathfrak a,0}(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k)\sum_{r\geq1}r^{k-3}q^{r\mathfrak a},
\]
and put $n_{\mathfrak a,0}=\mathrm{GW}_{\mathfrak a,0}$ when
$c_1(\mathfrak a)>0$. Then all these $n_{\mathfrak a,0}$ are integers.
head: environment
name: Ionel--Parker

label: thm:siebert
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:siebert}
Let $M$ be a complex projective manifold, $R\in H_2(M,\mathbb Z)$, and $g,k\geq0$.
On the moduli space $C_{R,g,k}(M)$ of genus-$g$, $k$-marked stable maps in
class $R$, the homology class associated to Behrend's algebraic virtual
fundamental class and Siebert's symplectic virtual fundamental class
coincide. In particular their numerical invariants with matching insertions
coincide.
head: environment
name: Siebert

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:CYcover} gives the smooth projective $n$-fold
$\widetilde Z$ with trivial canonical bundle. With any Kähler form,
it is a closed symplectic $2n$-manifold and $c_1=0$; hence it is
semipositive in the exact sense of Theorem~\ref{thm:IP}, in every
dimension under consideration.
The insertion $q^*\delta_0$ is integral and has complex codimension
$n-2$, the one-marked virtual dimension. Algebraic and symplectic invariants agree through
Theorem~\ref{thm:siebert} and the semipositive comparison convention
recorded above; this is a specified numerical comparison, not an assertion
equating every virtual-cycle construction.
Apply the one-primary formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:IP} to
$j_{+*}\beta$. Theorem~\ref{thm:CYcover} identifies its invariants,
insertions, and all effective covering roots with the local ones.
Uniqueness of the rational transform identifies its integral
coefficients with $b_\beta$. Finite summation gives $n_m$.
This proof does not use the quantum-$K$ identity.
head: environment
name: Symplectic proof with the semipositive convention

label: rem:truefake
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:truefake}
Let $\mathfrak M_\beta=\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,1}
(\widetilde Z,j_{+*}\beta)$ and use the insertion $\widetilde E_\delta$.
The fake invariant is the identity-sector Todd integral
\[
 \kappa_\beta^{\mathrm{fake}}
 :=\int_{[\mathfrak M_\beta]^{\mathrm{vir}}}
       \operatorname{ch}(\operatorname{ev}^*\widetilde E_\delta)\,
       \operatorname{Td}(T_{\mathfrak M_\beta}^{\mathrm{vir}})
 =N_{0,\beta}.
\]
The equality follows because the full Chern character is homogeneous
of exactly the virtual dimension, so only the constant Todd term
contributes. True quantum $K$-theory instead takes coherent cohomology
on the stack. The nonidentity inertia terms in the virtual
Kawasaki--Riemann--Roch calculation behind Theorem~\ref{thm:chou}
must be retained. Theorems~\ref{thm:integrality} and~\ref{thm:QK} give
\[
 \kappa_\beta-\kappa_\beta^{\mathrm{fake}}
 =\sum_{r\alpha=\beta}(r-r^{-2})b_\alpha.
\]
Primitivity of the total curve class alone does not exclude a boundary
map with a multiply-covered component and nontrivial automorphisms.
For a primitive class the displayed identity asserts that the total
nonidentity correction vanishes, not that every nonidentity stratum
is empty. Trivial stabilizers in the specific classes $e_i$ and
$e_i+e_j$ follow from the separate geometric descriptions in
Sections~\ref{sec:degreeone}--\ref{sec:degreetwo}.
head: environment
name: True and fake invariants, and boundary automorphisms

label: rem:integralambientlattice
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:integralambientlattice}
The compact-sector comparison transfers any insertion
$\eta\in H^{2n-4}(F_n,\mathbb Z)$ by $q^*\eta$. Rational ambientness, however,
does not imply that every such integral class is an integral combination
of the square-free monomials used in $E_\delta$. Here is a precise
lattice calculation. Poincar\'e duality, the integral weak-Lefschetz
identification, and the universal coefficient theorem identify
$H^{2n-4}(F_n,\mathbb Z)$ with the integral dual of $H^2(F_n,\mathbb Z)$, with coordinates
$\eta\mapsto(\int_{F_n}\eta p_j)_{j=1}^n$. For $|S|=n-2$,
\[
 \int_{F_n} p_Sp_j=\int_{Y_n} Hp_Sp_j
 =\begin{cases}1,&j\notin S,\\0,&j\in S.\end{cases}
\]
Thus a monomial with complement $\{a,b\}$ gives $e_a+e_b$.
These vectors generate the index-two sublattice
\[
 \{(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\in\mathbb Z^n:\textstyle\sum_i v_i\text{ is even}\}.
\]
Indeed their sums have even parity, whereas differences $e_i-e_j$
and the vectors $2e_i$ are integer combinations of pair sums; these
generate every vector of even total sum. The distinguished $\delta_0$
is itself the sum of these monomials, so its lift is unaffected.
This calculation neither rules out other integral $K$-lifts nor weakens
the primary theorem. It only prevents extending the displayed exact
algebraic lift to arbitrary integral insertions without a further
argument. The symplectic primary theorem concerns integral insertions
more generally; an exact algebraic quantum-$K$ expression for another
insertion must check its own Chern-character lift.
Corollary~\ref{ext:cor:vector} below nevertheless proves integral
coefficients of the full primary cover transform by pairing with integral
duals of coordinate curves.
head: environment
name: The integral ambient lattice for other insertions

label: cor:arithmeticbridge
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:arithmeticbridge}
Write $a_{n-2}(m)=[Q^m]h_{n-2}(Q)$. Unconditionally,
\[
 a_{n-2}(m)=-mN_m=-m\sum_{k\mid m}\frac{n_{m/k}}{k^2},
 \qquad
 h_{n-2}(Q)=\sum_{m\geq1}m n_m\log(1-Q^m),
\]
and
\[
 \exp(h_{n-2}(Q))=\prod_{m\geq1}(1-Q^m)^{m n_m}.
\]
Here rational powers mean their formal binomial expansions.
The $n_m$ are integral for every $n\geq4$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:primaryintegral}. The symbol $a_{n-2}$ is distinct from the
coefficient $d_{n-2}$ in the alternative period normalization.
head: environment
name: The highest logarithmic coefficient

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Use $h_{n-2}=-\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta$ and
$\theta_Q\operatorname{Li}_2(Q^m)=-m\log(1-Q^m)$.
At any fixed degree only finitely many factors contribute.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For $n=5$, $\dim_\mathbb C X_n=5$ and the primary insertion is $H^3/6$.
The exponent $k^{-2}$ comes from one primary marking, not from
the dimension of $X_n$. Formula~\eqref{eq:Li2} is a definitionally
invertible transformation of rational invariants. Integrality adds a
separate arithmetic assertion; it does not, by itself, identify the
coefficients with counts of embedded curves or with contributions of
individual covering loci. In particular no weight for the descendants
$\psi^a\delta_a$, $a>0$, follows from this primary transform. No
genus-one or higher-genus covering formula is asserted here.
head: environment
name: Interpretation for a Calabi--Yau fivefold

label: thm:fullambient
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fullambient}
For every $n\ge4$, every smooth $F_n\in|\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)|$, every positive
curve class $\beta$, and every $a\ge0$, the class defined by~\eqref{eq:Cdef} satisfies
\[
 C_{a,\beta}^\lambda\in
 \operatorname{im}\bigl(i^*:\operatorname{CH}^*(Y_n)_{\mathbb Q}
           \longrightarrow\operatorname{CH}^*(F_n)_{\mathbb Q}\bigr)[\lambda].
\]
Consequently every pairing with the Poincar\'e-orthogonal nonambient
cohomology vanishes. The ambient comparison~\eqref{eq:ambientpair}
identifies the full one-point evaluation classes in cohomology, and hence their
normalized one-point generating series in cohomology.
head: environment
name: Ambient one-point theory in Chow groups

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The universal hypersurface is a projective bundle over $Y_n$.
Chow localization and its projective-bundle formula imply that every
cycle defined over the entire smooth hypersurface family restricts to
an ambient cycle on each fiber. Appendix~\ref{app:structural} constructs
the universal virtual evaluation class and proves its specialization
by refined Gysin maps on the actual stable-map stacks. This verifies
the required universal-cycle hypothesis, including fixed curve classes
and nonreduced moduli spaces. Nondegeneracy of the ambient pairing in
Proposition~\ref{prop:ambient} then gives the full cohomological comparison.
head: environment

label: thm:minimalperiod
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:minimalperiod}
The operator $P_{n-1}$ of Definition~\ref{def:operator} is irreducible over
$\mathbb C(y)$ and has order $n-1$. Consequently every nonzero scalar differential
operator over $\mathbb C(y)$ annihilating $A(y)=\sum_{D\ge0}(-1)^Dc_Dy^D$ has order
at least $n-1$, so $P_{n-1}$ is the minimal operator of the period.
head: environment
name: Irreducibility and the minimal period equation

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Write $S_n=\mathscr S_n=\theta^{n+1}+\sum_{j\ge1}y^jU_j(\theta)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:operator}. Its cyclic module on $\mathbb G_m$ is the $n$th symmetric power of the rank-two connection $\theta^2+y=0$.
The monomial basis satisfies $\theta v_k=(n-k)v_{k+1}-kyv_{k-1}$, which gives exactly the defining recursion.
 The recursion makes \(v_0\) cyclic; the leading coefficient of \(S_n\) in
ordinary derivatives is \(y^{n+1}\), a unit on \(\mathbb G_m\), so the induced
surjection from its cyclic module to the rank-\((n+1)\) symmetric power is an
isomorphism. To identify this symmetric power with the connection considered
in~\cite{FSY}, first take the rank-two Kloosterman connection
\(\mathrm{Kl}_2\) of~\cite[Proposition~2.4(1)]{FSY}. In their coordinate \(z\),
it is the connection associated with
$
 (z\partial_z)^2-z.
$
After the change of coordinate \(z=-y\), one has
\(z\partial_z=y\partial_y=\theta\), so this operator becomes
$
 \theta^2+y.
$
Thus the rank-two connection occurring here is precisely the pullback of
\(\mathrm{Kl}_2\) under \(z=-y\). Consequently, the rank-\((n+1)\) connection
defined by \(S_n\) is the \(n\)-th symmetric power
\(\operatorname{Sym}^n\mathrm{Kl}_2\), after the same coordinate change.
Proposition~2.7 of~\cite{FSY} states that
\(\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathrm{Kl}_2\) is irreducible for every \(k\geq0\).
It follows that the cyclic module of \(S_n\) on \(\mathbb G_m\) is
irreducible.

For an operator $L=\theta^r+\sum_{j\ge1}y^jp_j(\theta)$, Lemma~\ref{irr:lem:extension} identifies $\mathscr D_{\mathbb A^1}/\mathscr D_{\mathbb A^1}(y^{-1}L)$ as a simple extension whenever the module on $\mathbb G_m$ is simple. Lemma~\ref{irr:lem:transform} identifies its Fourier transform, after restriction, inversion of the coordinate, and the gauge change $f=yg$, with
\[
 \mathfrak T(L)=\theta^{r-1}
   +\sum_{j\ge1}y^jp_j(\theta)\prod_{a=1}^{j-1}(\theta+a).
\]
A positive-order output is again simple. Apply this twice to $S_n$. The first output has order $n$, constant coefficient $\theta^n$, and nonconstant coefficients $U_j(\theta)\prod_{a=1}^{j-1}(\theta+a)$, by the bound $\deg U_j\le n+1-2j$. The second output is exactly $P_{n-1}$ and has order $n-1$. It is therefore irreducible over $\mathbb C(y)$.

Theorem~\ref{thm:PF} gives $P_{n-1}A=0$, and $A(0)=1$. The minimal annihilator of $A$ is a positive-order right divisor of $P_{n-1}$, so irreducibility forces its order to be $n-1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
On the diagonal, in our convention $I=1+\tau/z+O(z^{-2})$,
\[
 I^{0,\lambda}_{X_n}=1+\frac{HR-\lambda g(y)}{z}+O(z^{-2}).
\]
Thus $R$ is the divisor flat coordinate; its unit companion is
$-\lambda g(y)$, not $-\lambda R$. Equivalently these occur in the
$z^0$ coefficient of $zI$, not of $I$. The identity $A=\theta_yR$
identifies the derivative of this local mirror map with the fundamental
period of the quantum-Serre family. No identity of $\theta_QK_2$ with
$R$ is asserted.
head: environment
name: Which coefficient defines the mirror map

label: prop:physicaloperator
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:physicaloperator}
Let $\theta_s=s\partial_s$ and let $M_s$ denote multiplication by $s$.
Define the order-$n-1$ scalar operator
\[
 \mathscr L_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1} P_{n-1}(-1/s,-\theta_s)\circ M_s.
\]
Then $\mathscr L_{n-1} I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}=-n!$. Its coefficients in powers of
$\partial_s$ are polynomials in $s$, and its leading coefficient is
\[
 s^{n}\prod_{0\leq j<n/2}\left(1-\frac{(n-2j)^2}{s}\right).
\]
The period $\pi(s)=-yA(y)$, $y=-1/s$, is homogeneous for this operator.
head: environment
name: Change to the physical variable

title: Démonstration
body_md:
For any $f$ the operator is equivalently
\[
 (\mathscr L_{n-1} f)(s)=(-1)^{n}
 \left[P_{n-1}(y,\theta_y)\frac{f(-1/y)}y\right]_{y=-1/s}.
\]
Use~\eqref{eq:physicalPF} and $P_{n-1}A=0$ for the source and period.
The leading coefficient follows from~\eqref{eq:leadP} and the leading
term of $\theta_s^{n-1}=s^{n-1}\partial_s^{n-1}+\cdots$.
For polynomiality, write each nonconstant $y$-term in the algorithm as
$y^jQ_j(\theta_y)$, where $Q_j$ is divisible by
$\prod_{r=1}^{j-1}(\theta_y+r)^2$.
Composing with $M_s$ gives a constant multiple of
$s^{1-j}Q_j(-\theta_s-1)$. The latter polynomial in $\theta_s$ vanishes
at $0,\ldots,j-2$. Its expansion in the falling-factorial basis
$\theta_s(\theta_s-1)\cdots(\theta_s-r+1)=s^r\partial_s^r$
therefore starts at $r=j-1$. All powers $s^{r+1-j}$ are nonnegative.
The $j=0$ term is already polynomial.
head: environment

label: prop:firstcorrection
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:firstcorrection}
Put $\ell_T=\log T$ and
\[
 \mathsf F_{n-1}(\ell_T)=n![t^{n-1}]\exp(\ell_Tt)
     \exp\left(\sum_{r\geq1}\frac{2\zeta(2r+1)}{2r+1}t^{2r+1}\right).
\]
Primes below denote derivatives in $\ell_T$. Then, as $T\to+\infty$,
\[
 T I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(-T)=\mathsf F_{n-1}(\ell_T)+\frac{\mathsf C_{n-1}(\ell_T)}T
                  +O\bigl(T^{-2}(1+\ell_T)^{n-1}\bigr),
\]
where
\[
 \mathsf C_{n-1}=-n\mathsf F_{n-1}+(2n-2)\mathsf F_{n-1}'-(n-4)\mathsf F_{n-1}''-2\mathsf F_{n-1}'''.
\]
In particular, writing $\ell=\log T$ for these examples,
\begin{align*}
 \mathsf F_3&=4\ell^3+16\zeta(3),\\
 \mathsf C_3&=-16\ell^3+72\ell^2-48-64\zeta(3),\\
 \mathsf F_4&=5\ell^4+80\zeta(3)\ell,\\
 \mathsf C_4&=-25\ell^4+160\ell^3-60\ell^2-240\ell
                   -400\zeta(3)\ell+640\zeta(3).
\end{align*}
head: environment
name: Uniform first correction at large Euclidean momentum

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The degree-one coefficient of $e^{-H\log y}\mathcal I^{\sharp}(y,1)$ is
$-(1+H)^2\sum_i(1+p_i)^{-2}=-(1+H)^2(n-2H)$.
After the involution $\epsilon$ it becomes
$-n+(2n-2)H-(n-4)H^2-2H^3$.
Extract the top coefficient against $e^{H\ell_T}\widehat\Gamma_{X_n}$
and use $H^j e^{H\ell_T}=\partial_{\ell_T}^j e^{H\ell_T}$.
The remaining terms of the convergent logarithmic germ are bounded by
a constant times $T^{-2}(1+\ell_T)^{n-1}$ after multiplication by $T$.

label: ext:thm:primary
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Dimension-uniform primary extraction

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:division} and~\eqref{eq:Bdef}, the $z^{-2}$ coefficient
of the divided normalized series at $\lambda=0$ is the multivariable primary
evaluation series $\sum_{\beta>0}D_\beta\mathbf Q^\beta$, after restriction
to $F_n$. It may be computed in the square-free ambient ring before that
restriction. The linear part of the Euler-divided seed is
$g_{\mathbf d}\{(2h_{|\mathbf d|}-1/|\mathbf d|)H
-2\sum_i h_{d_i}p_i\}$. Normalization by $e^{-Hg}$ and the
term $(1-e^{-Hg})/H$ give the divisor-valued germ $\sum_i f_ip_i$.

It remains only to convert from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf Q$. For
$Q_i=x_ie^{g(\mathbf x)}$, multivariable coefficient extraction gives, for
any scalar germ $f$ with zero constant term,
\[
 [\mathbf Q^\beta]f(\mathbf x(\mathbf Q))
 = [\mathbf x^\beta]f(\mathbf x)e^{-|\beta|g(\mathbf x)}
      \det\!\left(\frac{\partial\log Q_i}{\partial\log x_j}\right)_{i,j}.
\]
The logarithmic Jacobian is a rank-one perturbation of the identity, so the
matrix determinant lemma gives
$\det(\partial\log Q_i/\partial\log x_j)=1+\Theta_xg$.
Applying this componentwise to $\sum_i f_ip_i$ proves
\eqref{ext:primaryextract}.
head: environment

label: ext:cor:vector
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{ext:cor:vector}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:IP}, every coefficient
of $B_\beta$ in the basis $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ is integral, for every $n\geq4$.
More generally, for integral even primary insertions whose total degree has the
required dimension, the local genus-zero transform with $\ell$ markings and
cover weight $r^{\ell-3}$ is integral.
head: environment
name: Integral primary vector

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:degreeone}, for each $i$ the class $e_i$ is represented by
a coordinate fiber $C_i\cong\mathbb P^1$ contained in $F_n$. Choose one such fiber
and let $\eta_i\in H^{2n-4}(F_n,\mathbb Z)$ be its integral Poincar\'e dual. Then
\[
 \int_Fp_j\eta_i=\int_{C_i}p_j=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Pull all insertions back by $q:\widetilde Z\to F_n$. The compact target is smooth projective
Calabi--Yau, and the compact-sector comparison identifies all marked virtual
theories and effective covering roots. Theorem~\ref{thm:IP}
therefore applies to the local sector. The transform with insertion
$\eta_i$ is precisely the $i$th coefficient of $B_\beta$.
No exact integral inverse Chern character for $\eta_i$ is assumed.
head: environment

label: ext:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{ext:main}
For every integer $n\geq1$, all ambient primitive endpoint limits
$C_j(\infty)$, $0\leq j\leq n$, exist along the positive Euclidean axis.
There are uniquely determined real numbers $b_1,\ldots,b_d$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{ext:mainformula}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n}C_j(\infty)H^j
  =G(H)\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{d}b_jH^j\right)\pmod{H^{n+1}}.
\end{equation}
The upper-half-plane contour identities used in the proof are equivalent
to the vanishing of the coefficients of $H^{d+1},\ldots,H^n$ in the
quotient on the right. As an affine linear system in $n$ finite-part
moments, they have rank $n-d=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$.
head: environment
name: All-loop endpoint reduction

label: ext:endpoint
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Modulo $p^2$, the Bessel defining series and its order derivative give
\[
 \sum_{a\geq0}\frac{(-z)^a}{\prod_{r=1}^a(p+r)^2}
 =\Gamma(1+2p)z^{-p}J_{2p}(2\sqrt z),\qquad
 J_{2p}(r)=J_0(r)+\pi pY_0(r).
\]
The derivative used here is~\cite[\S10.2(i), Eq.~(10.2.2), and \S10.15(iii), Eq.~(10.15.5)]{ext:DLMF}.
Represent $\Gamma(|\mathbf a|+1+H)^2$ by two Laplace integrals in $u,v$.
The powers of $yuv$ cancel, while
$\prod_i\Gamma(1+2p_i)=e^{-2\gamma H}$.
Termwise integration is legitimate for $0<y<n^{-2}$, using a majorant
with exponential part $e^{-u-v+2n\sqrt{yuv}}$ and polynomial logarithmic
factors. The product of the $n$ Bessel factors has coefficient $\mathscr B_j$ in
front of $H^j$. Integrating in $u$ at fixed $uv$, then setting
$r=2\sqrt{yuv}$, gives \eqref{ext:W}. Its exponentially convergent integral
continues the germ for every $x>0$.

For the primitive, set $w_x(r)=r\sqrt x K_1(r\sqrt x)$ and let $M_j(x)$ be
\eqref{ext:B} with $\mathscr B_j$ replaced by $w_x\mathscr B_j$, retaining the
same subtraction. Since $\theta_y w_x=xr^2K_0(r\sqrt x)/2$, the expression
\[
 P(H)\left(1+2H\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}M_j(x)H^j\right)
\]
has the required derivative.
This follows from the Mellin-transform identity
\begin{equation}
  2H\int_0^\infty w_x(r)e^{2H\ell(r)}\frac{\mathrm dr}{r}
  = e^{2\gamma H}\Gamma(1+H)^2x^{-H},
  \qquad \Re H>0,
\end{equation}
which is obtained from the standard Mellin transform
\cite[Eq.~(10.43.19)]{ext:DLMF}.
The Laurent pole of the integral is
$1/(2H)$; its finite coefficients use exactly the subtraction at $r_0$.
Multiplication by $P(H)$ gives $y^H$. The difference from the leading
small-$r$ terms is $O(y(1+|\log y|)^n)$, so \eqref{ext:normalization} is satisfied.
Finally $0<w_x\leq1$ and $w_x\to1$ as $x\downarrow0$.
After subtraction, near zero a uniform dominating function is
$Cr(1+|\log r|)^{n+1}$; at infinity use $|\mathscr B_j(r)|/r=O(r^{-1-n/2})$.
Dominated convergence proves \eqref{ext:C}. Expansion of $\log\Gamma$ and
Euler's sine product prove \eqref{ext:gamma} and the stated first coefficients.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
At $t=\mathrm i+z$,
\[
 p_k(\mathrm i+z)=(\mathrm i z)^k(2-\mathrm i z)^{n-k}.
\]
It has a zero of order exactly $k$, and
$p_k^{(k)}(\mathrm i)=k!\,\mathrm i^k2^{n-k}\neq0$.
Starting with $k=n$, equation \eqref{ext:jet} forces $a_n=0$.
Descending in $k$ forces
$a_{n-1}=\cdots=a_{\lceil n/2\rceil}=0$.
Conversely these vanishings make all equations \eqref{ext:jet} hold, because
all their lower derivatives vanish. They impose precisely $n-d$
independent conditions; the coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_d$ are arbitrary
in the solution space. The transformation from $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ to
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$ is affine triangular with diagonal entries $2$, so
it preserves rank and dimension. Lemma~\ref{ext:endpoint} gives existence of
the actual endpoint limits and identifies their quotient with $A$.
This proves \eqref{ext:mainformula} and the rank statement for every $n$.

label: ap:thm:ambient
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{ap:thm:ambient}
For every $n\geq4$, every smooth $F_n$ as above, every positive effective
$\beta$, and every $a\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{ap:eq:chowambient}
 C_{a,\beta}^\lambda\in
 \operatorname{im}\bigl(i^*:\operatorname{CH}^*(Y_n)_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\operatorname{CH}^*(F_n)_{\mathbb Q}\bigr)[\lambda].

in $\lambda$.

head: environment
name: Restriction of a universally defined cycle

label: ap:eq:pb
title: Démonstration
body_md:
The evaluation map of the globally generated line bundle is surjective:
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal K\longrightarrow V\otimes\mathcal O_{Y_n}
 \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The kernel $\mathcal K$ is a vector bundle of rank $N$.
The incidence variety is the bundle of lines in $\mathcal K$:
$\mathscr F=\mathbb P_{Y_n}(\mathcal K)$. We always use the lines convention:
$\mathbb P_{Y_n}(\mathcal K)=\operatorname{Proj}_{Y_n}\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal K^\vee)$.
In the quotient convention used in \cite[Tag~02TX]{Stacks}, this is
the projective bundle associated with $\mathcal K^\vee$; in both
descriptions $\mathcal O(1)$ is the dual tautological line.
In particular it is a smooth projective
variety, including above the locus of singular hypersurfaces. Its
relative hyperplane class is
\[
 \xi=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_{Y_n}(\mathcal K)}(1))
     =q^*c_1(\mathcal O_B(1)).
\]
The Chow localization sequence makes
$\operatorname{CH}^*(\mathscr F)_{\mathbb Q}\to\operatorname{CH}^*(\mathscr F_U)_{\mathbb Q}$ surjective.
Choose a lift $\bar\alpha$ of $\alpha$.
By the projective-bundle formula, every such lift can be written
\begin{equation}\label{ap:eq:pb}
 \bar\alpha=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\xi^j p^*\alpha_j,
 \qquad \alpha_j\in\operatorname{CH}^*(Y_n)_{\mathbb Q}.
\end{equation}
These two intersection-theoretic inputs are, respectively, the usual
localization sequence and the projective-bundle formula; see
\cite[Section 1.8 and Theorem 3.3]{Fulton}, and
\cite[Tag~02TX]{Stacks} for the latter.

Since $q|_{F_{n,s}}$ is constant, $\xi|_{F_{n,s}}=0$. Restricting~\eqref{ap:eq:pb} gives $\alpha|_{F_{n,s}}=i_s^*\alpha_0$.
The restriction is a refined pullback. The fiber inclusion is a regular
embedding because $q$ is smooth over $U$. Thus the argument applies
even when a chosen representative cycle does not meet $F_{n,s}$ properly.

title: Remark
body_md:
The lemma concerns cycles that exist on the entire universal family
over $U$. An arbitrary cycle on one special fiber need not have this
property. This is exactly the issue that must be checked for~\eqref{ap:eq:C}; it is not enough to invoke permutation symmetry or to
declare that a class is deformation invariant.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For the zero stack, the relative two-term complex over $U$ is
$[\mathcal E^\vee|_{\mathscr M}\to
\Omega_{\mathcal A/U}|_{\mathscr M}]$, in degrees $[-1,0]$.
Its fiber gives the zero-locus obstruction theory used in~\eqref{ap:eq:KKPfiber}. The absolute complex instead contains
$\Omega_{\mathcal A}$ and hence the parameter-space cotangent
directions from $\Omega_U$. Its ordinary restriction to a fiber
is not the absolute obstruction theory of $M_{F_{n,s}}$.
The conclusion needed here is the refined equality~\eqref{ap:eq:fiberVFC}, proved by the two steps above.
head: environment
name: Relative and absolute obstruction theories

title: Remark
body_md:
Adjunction on the universal family gives
$K_{\mathscr F_U/U}=\mathcal O_{Y_n}(-H)|_{\mathscr F_U}\otimes q^*\mathcal O_U(1)$.
We deliberately used the globally fixed line bundle
$\mathcal O_{Y_n}(-H)$ in~\eqref{ap:eq:universalC}. On a fiber the extra factor
is a constant one-dimensional vector space, and has zero Chern class;
the resulting Euler classes agree with~\eqref{ap:eq:C}. Thus no
trivialization of $\mathcal O_U(1)$ over the parameter space is being
assumed.
head: environment
name: Relative canonical bundles

title: Remark
body_md:
Choosing one lift of each coefficient of $\mathscr C_a^\lambda$ to
$\mathscr F$ in Lemma~\ref{ap:lem:universal} produces a polynomial
$\alpha_{a,\mathbf d}(\lambda)\in\operatorname{CH}^*(Y_n)_{\mathbb Q}[\lambda]$ such that
$i_s^*\alpha_{a,\mathbf d}(\lambda)=C_{a,\beta_s}^\lambda$ for every
$s\in U$. The ambient polynomial need not be unique, but the argument
works simultaneously for all smooth fibers.

name: A uniform lift

label: ap:prop:invariants
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ap:prop:invariants}
For every $k$ and $s\in U$,
\[
 H^k(F_{n,s},\mathbb Q)^{\pi_1(U,s)}=i_s^*H^k(Y_n,\mathbb Q).
\]
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Apply the global invariant-cycle theorem to
$q:\mathscr F\to B$. Both spaces are smooth projective varieties,
$B$ is connected, $q$ is surjective, and its restriction over $U$ is
smooth and proper. The theorem identifies the invariant subspace
with the image of $H^k(\mathscr F,\mathbb Q)$ in $H^k(F_{n,s},\mathbb Q)$; see
\cite[Theorem 3.3]{Voisin}. The cohomological projective-bundle
formula writes every class on $\mathscr F$ in powers of $\xi$ with
coefficients from $Y_n$. Restricting to $F_{n,s}$ kills every positive power
of $\xi$. This proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: ap:cor:fullJ
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{ap:cor:fullJ}
Suppose an ambient class $E_{a,\beta}^\lambda\in H^*(Y_n)[\lambda]$
satisfies
\[
 \int_{F_n} i^*b\,C_{a,\beta}^\lambda
 =\int_{F_n} i^*b\,i^*E_{a,\beta}^\lambda
 \quad\text{for all }b\in H^*(Y_n).
\]
Then $C_{a,\beta}^\lambda=i^*E_{a,\beta}^\lambda$ in cohomology.
Thus a comparison against ambient insertions determines the full
one-point evaluation classes. It also determines every generating
series formed from them, in particular the one-point $J$-series
once its normalization is fixed.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The difference is ambient by Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:ambient}, and is
orthogonal to the ambient space by the displayed equality.
Nondegeneracy makes the difference zero. Apply this coefficientwise
in $\lambda$ and then in the Novikov and descendant variables.

label: irr:lem:extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{irr:lem:extension}
Let $r\ge1$ and
\[
 L=\theta^r+\sum_{j\ge1}t^jp_j(\theta),\qquad p_j\in\mathbb C[\theta].
\]
Suppose $\mathscr D^\times/\mathscr D^\times L$ is nonzero and simple. Then
\[
 B=t^{-1}L=\partial_t\theta^{r-1}
             +\sum_{j\ge1}t^{j-1}p_j(\theta)\in\mathscr D,
 \qquad M=\mathscr D/\mathscr D B
\]
is simple. More precisely, $M$ has neither a nonzero submodule nor a nonzero quotient supported at $t=0$, and restricts to $\mathscr D^\times/\mathscr D^\times L$.
head: environment
name: The extension used in each transform

label: irr:eq:noquot
title: Démonstration
body_md:
The order in which the factors are written is important. Let $v=\sum_{k=0}^Nc_ke_k\in\delta_0$ with $c_N\ne0$. The first term of $Bv$ has coefficient
\[
 c_N(-N-1)^{r-1}\ne0
\]
at $e_{N+1}$. Each remaining term $t^{j-1}p_j(\theta)v$ has degree at most $N$ in $\partial_t$. Thus $B$ acts injectively on $\delta_0$, and
\begin{equation}\label{irr:eq:noquot}
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr D}(M,\delta_0)=0.
\end{equation}

Let $*$ denote formal transpose, such that $t^*=t$, $\partial_t^*=-\partial_t$, and $(UV)^*=V^*U^*$. Since $\theta^*=-\theta-1$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{irr:eq:transpose}
 B^*=(-1)^r\partial_t\theta^{r-1}
       +\sum_{j\ge1}t^{j-1}p_j(-\theta-j).
\end{equation}
The same highest-degree calculation shows that $B^*$ acts injectively on $\delta_0$.

This also proves directly, without invoking holonomic duality, that
multiplication by $t$ is injective on $M$. Indeed, suppose $t[U]=0$. Then
$tU=VB$ for some $V\in\mathscr D$, whence
\[
 U^*t=B^*V^*.
\]
Apply this equality to $e\in\delta_0$. Injectivity of $B^*$ gives $V^*e=0$, so
$V^*=Wt$ for some $W\in\mathscr D$. Transposition yields $V=tW^*$. Since the
Weyl algebra is a domain, cancellation in $tU=tW^*B$ gives $U=W^*B$ and $[U]=0$.

It follows that $M$ has no nonzero $t$-torsion submodule. It has no
nonzero quotient supported at zero either. Indeed, such a quotient would
be a nonzero module with locally nilpotent $t$ and hence would have a
quotient $\delta_0$, contrary to~\eqref{irr:eq:noquot}.


Finally let $N\subset M$ be a nonzero submodule. Its localization is nonzero, by
the absence of $t$-torsion, and therefore is the entire localization of $M$ by
the assumed simplicity. Thus $M/N$ is supported at zero, and must vanish. Hence
$M$ is simple.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In the language of holonomic modules, the lemma identifies this presentation
with the intermediate extension at zero. Using $L$ itself as a polynomial
Weyl-algebra presentation, rather than $t^{-1}L$, would not justify that
assertion.

title: Lemma

name: Explicit transformed operator

label: irr:eq:fourierB
title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{irr:lem:extension}, $M=\mathscr D/\mathscr D(t^{-1}L)$ is simple. Its Fourier transform has cyclic presentation by
\begin{equation}\label{irr:eq:fourierB}
 \mathscr F(B)=x(-\theta_x-1)^{r-1}
          +\sum_{j\ge1}(-\partial_x)^{j-1}p_j(-\theta_x-1).
\end{equation}
Restrict to $x\ne0$ and invert the coordinate, $x=1/y$. Then
\[
 \theta_x=-\theta_y,\qquad -\partial_x=y\theta_y,
 \qquad (y\theta_y)^k=y^k\prod_{a=0}^{k-1}(\theta_y+a).
\]
Thus \eqref{irr:eq:fourierB} becomes
\[
 C=y^{-1}(\theta_y-1)^{r-1}
     +\sum_{j\ge1}y^{j-1}
       \left(\prod_{a=0}^{j-2}(\theta_y+a)\right)p_j(\theta_y-1).
\]
The rational gauge change $f(y)=y\,g(y)$ replaces $C$ by $y^{-1}Cy$. Multiplying on the left by the unit $y$ then gives precisely
\[
 y\bigl(y^{-1}Cy\bigr)=\mathfrak T(L).
\]
These equalities take place in the localized Weyl algebra, with all products in
their stated order. In particular they identify the cyclic modules.

Positive differential order implies that the final cyclic module has nonzero generic rank. Thus the restriction of $\mathscr F(M)$ to $x\ne0$ was nonzero. The localization observation, coordinate inversion, and the gauge isomorphism prove simplicity. The same observation applies on passing to $\mathbb C(y)$.
